title: New Mexico Court Orders Meta to Pay $942 Million in Landmark Child Safety Ruling
excerpt: A judge added $567 million in abatement costs on top of the earlier $375 million jury verdict, making it the largest child safety penalty against a social media company.
body:
• A New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay $567 million into a child mental health fund, on top of a $375 million jury verdict from March, bringing the total to $942 million.
  • Meta must delete accounts of users under 13, turn off push notifications during school hours, and set teen accounts to private by default in New Mexico.
  • The judge compared Meta's platforms to polluting factories and declared them a public nuisance harming children and families.
  • Meta said it disagrees with the ruling and plans to appeal.

A New Mexico judge on Thursday ordered Meta to pay $567 million into a state fund to address the mental health crisis among teenagers using its platforms, adding to a $375 million penalty a jury had already imposed in March. The combined $942 million makes it the largest child safety ruling against a social media company in U.S. history.

Beyond Fines: Sweeping Platform Changes

Judge Bryan Biedscheid's ruling goes well beyond monetary penalties. Among the most significant requirements, according to CNN and the Wall Street Journal:

https://youtube.com/watch?v=PuBrV0glwUY

Meta must delete all accounts and personal information belonging to users under 13 in New Mexico. The company must turn off push notifications during school hours — 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. on weekdays during the school year — and between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. on all other days for users under 18.

Teen accounts in New Mexico must automatically be set to private. Meta must also prevent New Mexico users from engaging in romantic or sexualized interactions with its artificial intelligence chatbots.

"Just as noxious pollution produced by a factory can harm the common public right to reasonably clean air, the harmful effects of Meta's platforms on children do not stay contained by its platforms and, instead, migrate to the internet as a whole and, perhaps most concerning, to the real world."

— Judge Bryan Biedscheid, New Mexico First Judicial District Court

How the Case Unfolded

The case was filed in 2023 by New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who accused Meta of creating a "breeding ground" for child predators on Facebook and Instagram. It grew out of an undercover investigation in which state agents created decoy accounts posing as children under 14. Those accounts were sent sexually explicit material and solicited for sex by several adults who were later arrested, according to TechCrunch.

A jury in March found Meta liable on all counts under the state's Unfair Practices Act, including willfully engaging in "unfair and deceptive" and "unconscionable" trade practices. That verdict — at $5,000 per violation for approximately 75,000 violations — yielded the $375 million penalty.

Thursday's ruling addressed the second phase of the trial, in which the judge determined whether Meta's platforms constituted a "public nuisance." The $567 million abatement fund was smaller than the $779.5 million state attorneys had sought but was deemed "necessary, due to the wide-ranging impacts of the harm and the complex nature of the remedy," according to the Wall Street Journal.

Implications for the Tech Industry

Meta faces thousands of similar lawsuits from state attorneys general, school districts, and individual plaintiffs alleging the company prioritized growth over the safety of young users. The New Mexico case was the first to go to trial and test whether social media companies should be held financially responsible for content on their platforms, according to Reuters.

A separate jury is deliberating in Los Angeles after a trial in which CEO Mark Zuckerberg denied that Meta's platforms were designed to be addictive for children.

"We remain confident in our record of protecting teens online and will continue to defend ourselves against claims that misrepresent the facts," a Meta spokesman said, confirming the company plans to appeal.

What This Means for Users

If the ruling survives appeal, New Mexico would become the first state to impose enforceable platform-design changes on Meta specifically targeting child users. The notification restrictions and mandatory private accounts could serve as a template for other states pursuing similar litigation. For Indian American parents, the case underscores growing momentum to hold platforms accountable for child safety — a concern that transcends borders.

What's Next

Meta's appeal will likely focus on challenging the public nuisance finding and the scope of the platform changes ordered. The company's legal exposure continues to expand as similar cases move toward trial in other states. The outcome could shape how social media platforms operate for young users across the United States for years to come.
